title: Of books
hookLine: he reads for pleasure and puts down any book that bores him (Essays 2.10)

cards: A bookmark that hasn't moved since spring. It sits in a book on the nightstand, a book you were told was important, and every night it gets a little heavier with guilt.

Close by, maybe, another book you'd actually love to read is waiting its turn. Montaigne kept a library at the top of his tower, and in his essay Of Books, he tells us exactly what he does with the ones that bore him.
He doesn't feel bad about it.

teach.b: First, why he reads. Montaigne says he looks for nothing in books except pleasure, honest amusement. Or, if he studies, he looks only for the learning that teaches him to know himself, and to live well and die well.
That's his whole reading list: delight, or wisdom he can use. Second, no biting nails. When he hits something hard in a book, he doesn't bite his nails over it.

teach.h: A CHARGE OR TWO, THEN LEAVE IT.
teach.b: He gives it a charge or two, and if it won't open, he leaves it; pushing harder only clouds his mind. And if a book bores him, he picks up another.

teach.h: BOOKS YOU CAN PICK UP AND PUT DOWN.

teach.b: He's fond of Plutarch and Seneca, partly because their writing comes in separate pieces: you can start, stop, and come back, without a long commitment.
And he confesses, a little daringly, that Cicero's long warm-ups, the definitions and divisions before the point, wear him out. He wants to get to the meat. Fourth, notes at the back.
Montaigne's memory was bad, and he says so. So he wrote a short verdict at the end of a book, so he wouldn't pick it up later thinking it was new. That small habit matters.
Reading for joy isn't careless reading.
He wanted what he read to stay with him and change how he lived. Read for joy might mean closing the book you're dragging through, and opening one that wakes you up.

how: Readers of Montaigne often borrow his rule for their own shelves: read for honest pleasure or for what helps you live, and feel free to set aside what does neither.

games.q: you're Montaigne, and the book in your hands has stopped making sense. what do you do?
o: bite your nails and push through to the end.
give it a charge or two, then leave it for another book.
copy it out until you understand it.
games.why: he says pushing harder only clouds his mind. if a book bores him, he picks up another.

practice: Bring to mind what you're reading, watching or listening to out of duty, a book, a series, a podcast, a pile of articles, and hold one of them up to Montaigne's two questions. Does it give me honest pleasure?
Does it teach me how to live? If both answers are no, picture setting it back on the shelf without guilt, and let one thing come to mind that you'd read with real joy.

wordCard.voice: Of books. Montaigne reads for honest pleasure or for what teaches him to live and die well, and when a book bores him, he picks up another. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: read for joy. Delight is a good enough reason to open a book. Go gently.
